strengths: Clean architectural idea: augmenting every transformer layer with a dedicated, bounded external memory track (mem2tok/tok2mem cross-attention plus an LRU-based replace/blend update) that is simple to implement and interpret.

Provides a theoretical analysis (exponential forgetting, half-life, boundedness) that gives some formal grounding to the design choices of the LRU update rule, unlike most memory-augmented RL papers that are purely empirical.

Broad empirical coverage across three qualitatively different testbeds (synthetic T-Maze, 48 POPGym tasks, MIKASA-Robo visual manipulation), with a reasonably diverse baseline set (DT, RATE, DMamba, BC, CQL, DP).

Strong extrapolation results on T-Maze (100% success up to 1M-step corridors from L=10, S=3 training) and a fairly thorough ablation study isolating memory size, blending factor, initialization, and segment configuration.

Reports efficiency numbers (parameter count, inference latency) showing the memory mechanism adds little overhead versus DT/RATE, and includes a sanity check on CartPole-v1 confirming memory does not hurt fully observable performance.
weaknesses: Inconsistent reporting of POPGym results: the abstract/main text claims ELMUR is best on '24 of 48' tasks ('more than half'), while the actual Table 4 caption states results on 21 tasks with ELMUR best on only 12 — these numbers should match and the discrepancy undermines confidence in the reported headline claim.

The T-Maze task requires retaining only a single binary cue, so the '100,000x' and 'one million steps' claims, while striking, may be an artifact of the task's minimal information content (LRU memory with enough capacity trivially solves single-bit recall); it is unclear this generalizes to tasks requiring richer, evolving memory content.

The ablation shows that removing the MoE-FFN and replacing it with a plain MLP-FFN preserves accuracy exactly (1.00 vs 1.00) while improving efficiency, which undercuts the motivation for including DeepSeek-MoE in the main architecture and suggests the design choice is not well justified by the evidence presented.

Memory capacity M must be matched to the (often unknown a priori) number of segments N required to solve a task, as shown starkly in the ablations (Figure 6c-d); this is a practical limitation for real-world deployment where horizon length is not known in advance, and the paper does not propose or test any adaptive/growing memory scheme.

Many individual results have large variance/overlapping error bars relative to baselines (e.g., TakeItBack RATE 0.42±0.24 vs ELMUR 0.78±0.03; several POPGym tasks where RATE or BC-LSTM outperform ELMUR), and only 3–4 seeds per condition are used, limiting statistical confidence in the 'consistent' superiority claims.

MIKASA-Robo evaluation is limited to only 4 tasks from one benchmark family, and absolute success rates remain fairly low (0.19–0.89), so the 'nearly doubles baseline performance' claim, while numerically true in places, describes modest absolute capability on manipulation under visual partial observability.

The relative bias mechanism clamps offsets to a fixed maximum distance Dmax, which is in tension with the paper's headline claims of unbounded/arbitrary-horizon generalization — the practical bounds and behavior beyond Dmax are not clearly discussed.

Baseline sets are inconsistent across benchmarks (e.g., RMT and TrXL appear only in the T-Maze figure but not in the POPGym/MIKASA-Robo tables), making cross-benchmark comparisons of relative strength harder to interpret.

No real-robot or online-RL evaluation is provided (acknowledged as a limitation), and the offline imitation-learning setup with expert-generated datasets may not fully capture challenges of noisier, more realistic data regimes.

strengths: Proposes a well-motivated architecture (ELMUR) that equips every transformer layer with its own external memory track, bidirectional mem2tok/tok2mem cross-attention, and a principled LRU-based update rule (replacement + convex blending), addressing a clear gap in long-horizon partially observable decision making.

Provides rigorous theoretical analysis (Propositions 1 and 2) with full proofs establishing exponential forgetting rates, half-life bounds, and boundedness of memory embeddings under the convex update rule, connecting theory to the empirically observed retention horizons.

Extremely broad empirical evaluation spanning synthetic T-Maze (up to 1M-step corridors, 100,000x context extension), 48 POPGym tasks, 32 MIKASA-Robo visual manipulation tasks, D4RL MuJoCo MDPs, and ViZDoom-Two-Colors 3D navigation, with strong and consistent baselines (DT, RATE, DMamba, CQL, DP, BC).

Very thorough ablation and interpretability studies in the appendix (memory probing with linear classifiers, PCA analysis, cross-attention visualization, memory update pattern heatmaps) that provide compelling mechanistic evidence that the model performs genuine, causally relevant long-term storage rather than merely benefiting from added parameters.

Reasonable efficiency profile relative to baselines (comparable parameter count, faster per-step latency than RATE/DT) despite the added memory machinery, and inclusion of an MoE-vs-MLP ablation showing efficiency gains without accuracy loss.
Reproducibility statement, detailed hyperparameter tables, and stated code/data availability support replication.
weaknesses: Reported POPGym results are internally inconsistent: the main text/abstract claims a top score on '24 of 48' (also stated as 'more than half') tasks, while the caption of the detailed results table (Table 5) states ELMUR is best on '12' of '21 partially observable tasks,' and the aggregate score table differs slightly (9.5/10.4 vs 9.54/10.41) — this discrepancy undermines confidence in the reported comparative statistics.

On MIKASA-Robo, a large fraction of tasks (BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors, ChainOfColors — 9 of 32 tasks) show 0.00 success for every method including ELMUR, meaning the headline '21 of 23 tasks' and '~70% aggregate improvement' claims are computed only over a subset of tasks where any method succeeds at all, which could overstate the practical significance of the gains and obscures that a third of the tasks remain entirely unsolved by all approaches.

On POPGym reactive/control tasks, ELMUR's advantage over DT/RATE/BC-LSTM is marginal (9.2 vs 9.1–9.3), and it is not uniformly the best method across categories, suggesting the gains are concentrated in memory-intensive puzzle tasks rather than a universal improvement.

The dramatic '100,000x' extrapolation claim is derived from a specific favorable configuration (L=10, S=3) on a synthetic, low-dimensional T-Maze task; the practical relevance of such extreme extrapolation to realistic robotic settings with rich, noisy, high-dimensional observations is not established, and no similarly extreme long-horizon stress test is performed on MIKASA-Robo or real-world-like data.

The architecture adds non-trivial complexity (per-layer memory tracks, dual cross-attention blocks, LRU bookkeeping with anchors, MoE FFNs, relative-bias tables) relative to simpler baselines like RATE or DT, and while latency is reported as comparable, a more complete compute/memory-footprint comparison (e.g., training time, FLOPs, wall-clock scaling with M and number of layers) is not provided.

No real-robot or truly high-fidelity long-horizon manipulation benchmark is used (acknowledged as a limitation), and comparisons to more recent, directly competing memory-augmented VLA/manipulation methods discussed in related work (e.g., MemoryVLA, SAM2Act+) are only qualitative, not empirical, leaving open how ELMUR compares to the most relevant contemporary memory-augmented manipulation baselines.

The ablation study's reported 'Score' metric (Table 3) is not clearly defined (e.g., which exact metric, over how many seeds, and whether it matches the success-rate metric used elsewhere), reducing clarity of this section.
